extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent practitioners and support staff (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for identifying and using prior art, conducting searches, classifying patent documents (USPC/CPC), and routing/assigning patent applications within the USPTO. Covers what counts as a reference, how to obtain and order files, foreign-document considerations, kind/INID codes, and classification challenge/transfer procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canceled Matter in U.S. Patent Files
rubrics_metrics.description: Canceled matter in the application file of a U.S. patent or U.S. application publication is not a proper reference as of the filing date under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter canceled from the application file wrapper of a U.S. patent or U.S. application publication may be used as prior art as of the patent or publication date, respectively, because it then constitutes prior public knowledge or prior public availability under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a). See Ex parte Stalego, In re Lund, and MPEP §§ 2127 and 2136.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of Patented and Abandoned Application Files
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for obtaining patented or abandoned application files (IFW vs paper) and the File Ordering System (FOS) statuses for file requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners can view IFW files via the Patent Examiner's Toolkit. Paper files are ordered via FOS which requires art unit, employee number, and patent/application numbers. FOS responses indicate: (A) accepted; (B) accepted but at remote warehouse; (C) not accepted — file not located at repository/warehouse; (D) not accepted — previous request not yet filled; (E) not accepted — invalid number. Files Repository personnel retrieve, deliver, and return files per request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned Applications as Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: A previously published abandoned application (published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)) is prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), 102(b) and 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as of its publication date; it may be available as pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as of its earliest effective U.S. filing date and under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as of its effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not redacted, the specification, drawings and papers of an abandoned published application are open to public inspection under 37 CFR 1.11(a) and thus can be used as prior art as of public availability. Unpublished abandoned applications whose file contents become public under 37 CFR 1.14 may also be used as prior art as of the date the subject matter became publicly available. Published abstracts, abbreviatures, defensive publications, and statutory invention registrations are references (see MPEP § 901.06(d) and Chapter 1100).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of Pending Unpublished Applications and Publication Exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending U.S. applications that have not been published are generally confidential and are not available as references, subject to enumerated exceptions and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except as provided in 37 CFR 1.11(b), 1.14(a)(1)(v), and 1.14(a)(1)(vi), unpublished pending applications are preserved in confidence under 37 CFR 1.14(a). However, claims in one nonprovisional application may be rejected based on a copending nonprovisional application of the same inventive entity (see MPEP § 804). AIPA (effective Nov 29, 1999) requires publication generally 18 months after earliest filing date unless exceptions apply. An application shall not be published if it is: (A) no longer pending; (B) under secrecy order (35 U.S.C. 181); (C) a provisional application (35 U.S.C. 111(b)); (D) a design patent application (35 U.S.C. 171); (E) an international design application (35 U.S.C. 382); or (F) a reissue application (35 U.S.C. 251). Applicants may request nonpublication at filing (see MPEP § 1122).

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Patents: Series, Citation, and Effective Prior Art Dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Different historical series and types of U.S. patents exist (X-series, 1836 series, reissue, A.I., plant, design, etc.), and the date to cite and the effective prior art date may vary (filing date, issue date, or earlier effective U.S. filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date of patenting on the face is usually the publication date and commonly cited; filing date often is the effective prior-art date. Reissue patents have separate numbering and the effective date as a reference is that of the original patent application. See MPEP §§ 2127, 2136, and 2154 for pre-AIA 102(e) and 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) date rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates After Issuance and Their Effect on Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Certificates issued after patent grant (reexamination certificates, certificates of correction, post-grant review/inter partes review/derivation certificates) affect the patent record and prior art dates in specified ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexamination certificates indicate changes to the specification/claims; changes may not enlarge claim scope; prior art dates remain those of the reexamined patent. Certificates of correction are part of the original patent and do not change prior art dates. PTAB post-grant review or inter partes review certificates issued following final decisions will cancel or confirm claims and incorporate any new/amended patentable claims—these certificates are published and affect the patent record. Derivation certificates can cancel claims if PTAB determines derivation. See 35 U.S.C. 254–255, 307, pre-AIA 316, and related MPEP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: INID Codes for Bibliographic Data Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: INID (Internationally agreed Numbers for the Identification of (bibliographic) Data) codes identify bibliographic data on the first page of patent documents without language knowledge and are used on U.S. patents since Aug 4, 1970.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all INID codes apply to every country/document. For a list see MPEP § 901.05(b). USPTO documents are recommended to be identified by three elements: (A) two-character country code (US); (B) patent or publication number; and (C) WIPO ST.16 kind code (e.g., “US 7,654,321 B1”, “US 2003/1234567 A1”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kind Codes (WIPO ST.16) Usage and Citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Kind codes (WIPO ST.16) are letters/numbers used to distinguish the kind and level of patent documents (e.g., application publication, patent, corrected publication) and to indicate a document's publication status/level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since Jan 2, 2001 USPTO prints WIPO ST.16 codes. Examples: A1/A2 for patent application publications, B1/B2 for patents (with/without previously published application), C1/C2 for reexamination certificates. AIA trial-related codes (J, K, O) are used for Post-Grant Review, Inter Partes Review, and Derivation Certificates respectively. Always include country code, number, and kind code when identifying documents; application publication numbers include the year and a seven-digit number starting at 0000001 each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Patent Documents: Use as References and Date Confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patents, published applications, and other published derivative material disseminated to the public are available to U.S. examiners as references, but an examiner should confirm the date of patenting or public availability before citing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some countries delay publication between grant and publication, examiners should confirm the patent/publication date by reviewing a copy of the document. See MPEP §§ 901.06(a) and 901.08. Information on major source countries is in MPEP § 901.05(a) and obtainable from the Scientific and Technical Information Center (STIC). See also MPEP § 707.05(e) for data used in citing foreign references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview of Foreign Patent Law Variations That Affect Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patent systems vary in applicant nomenclature, what 'application' means, timing and form of publication of pending applications, administrative systems (examining vs registration), opposition systems, patent grant practices, and patent maintenance/term rules — all of which affect availability and dating of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in many countries the applicant (often assignee) may differ from inventor; some countries 'lay open' applications for inspection rather than publish full specifications; some publish specifications 18 months after filing; some countries have opposition periods after an allowance; patent events (grant, publication, availability) occur on different dates across countries and must be considered when determining prior art dates under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b)/(a)(1) and 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)/(e). See In re Wyer and related MPEP paragraphs for publication-as-reference guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Patent Family and External Databases for Determining Corresponding Foreign Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When a corresponding foreign patent or application might establish an earlier date, examiners should search family members and external databases (Derwent World Patents Index, INPADOC, Chemical Abstracts) to locate earlier publications or grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derwent, INPADOC, and Chemical Abstracts (CAS) can show family members, cross-references, and abstracts; CAS abstracts chemical patents and references one family member in full. Chemical Abstracts access procedures via STIC are provided. Checking family members can reveal earlier printed publication dates or issue dates that affect effective prior art dates (e.g., earlier foreign publication predating a U.S. filing date). See MPEP § 2154.01(b) for determinations related to foreign priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding Specifications in a Family and Priority Right Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in different countries for the same invention form a family and priority rights (Paris Convention) allow later filings within one year to claim benefit of earlier filing dates; corresponding specifications may be identical, translations, or differ (e.g., continuation-in-part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a U.S. patent or published application that claims foreign priority, determine whether the foreign application issued or published earlier — this can provide an earlier effective date. Use 35 U.S.C. 102(d) to decide whether a foreign priority can be used as an 'effectively filed' date. Duplicate or translated specifications may be cited; content questions are settled based on the specification actually used as the reference. See MPEP § 213 and § 2154 for priority and effective-date rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Analysis for Search: Variant Embodiments, Equivalents, and Analogous Arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Search must be driven by careful analysis of the claims, identifying variant embodiments within claim scope, potential equivalents, and analogous arts relevant to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claim language and disclosure to determine scope and embodiments to search. Consider doctrine of equivalents and analogous arts where appropriate. Use claim analysis to select classification areas, keywords, and search strategies; see MPEP guidance sections on how to search and analyze claims for search planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Search Guidelines and Tool Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for selecting search tools (classified vs. electronic), conducting internet searches, and searching related post-grant proceedings, including use of automated tools like PE2E and CPC databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose classified search when appropriate; select search tool(s) based on subject matter (CPC, USPC, nonpatent literature databases). Use CPC definitions, guidance headings, and warnings in CPC schemes; exploit CPC database and combination sets. Consider searches of post-grant proceedings and international databases. Use PE2E and other automated search tools as available and appropriate. Document search strategy and results in the file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) Scheme and Classification Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach to classification in CPC: use CPC titles, definitions, guidance headings, notes, and combination sets; CPC symbols must represent claimed subject matter and certain CPC entries may carry warnings or guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should use CPC titles, references within titles, notes, warnings, and guidance headings found in CPC schemes to determine proper classification. CPC definitions and combination sets can direct search scope. A C* (C-Star) binary designation is used at the family level to mark CPC symbols that are representative of the claimed subject matter — these influence routing/assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: C* (C-Star) Designations and Automated Routing of Applications in CPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonprovisional utility application must be fully classified with C* designations assigned to CPC symbols that represent the subject matter claimed; automated routing uses these classifications and C* to assign an examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The automated routing system compares application CPC classifications (including C* symbols) to examiner portfolios and weights additional factors such as docket size, backlogs, and continuation/divisional status to assign the best available examiner. Provisional applications are not classified or assigned. C* denotes family-level CPC symbols representative of claimed subject matter (see MPEP § 905.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification Challenge (C* Challenge) Procedure via CAT
rubrics_metrics.description: If an assigned examiner believes one or more C* designations are incorrect, they must initiate a C* classification challenge using the Classification Allocation Tool (CAT), providing explanations and suggested additions/removals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete the CAT C* challenge form with all challenges and reasons. If unable to determine appropriate C* designations, consult a supervisory patent examiner, search/classification expert, or quality nominee. If management determines changes and a First Action on the Merits (FAOM) has not been credited, the application may be rerouted based on new C* designations. If management makes no change, the application remains with assigned examiner and a brief explanation is provided. CAT pages create a record of classification challenge history and are used for patent file wrapper documentation. See MPEP § 909.01(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate Inspection of Amendments Affecting Classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When receipt of an amendment makes a classification (C*) challenge necessary, prompt action must be taken per the C* challenge procedure; generally C* will not be removed once a FAOM has been mailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act promptly upon amendments that change claimed subject matter; initiate CAT challenge and follow procedures in MPEP § 909.01(d). If FAOM has been mailed, C* removal is generally not done afterward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment, Transfer, and Transfer Procedure in USPC for Design and Plant Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for transferring applications between examiners/art units under USPC: initiation, classification attempts, communications, acceptance, and dispute resolution paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner believes an application is misplaced, they should determine proposed classification (may perform cursory search or contact applicant), then email the receiving examiner with full explanation. If the receiving examiner accepts, they classify and assign. If examiners cannot agree, forward to supervisors; unresolved disputes go to the TC 2900 docketing POC for a final decision. Plant applications (35 U.S.C. 161) are assigned to AU 1661 and rerouted if misrouted.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Guidelines Governing Assignment of Nonprovisional Design and Plant Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are generally assigned based on where the application would have an original classification if the claims were in a patent, following rules/principles of classification (MPEP § 903.07) and various assignment criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: (A) assignment follows classification principles as much as possible; (B) criteria for original classification are in MPEP § 903.07; (C) read claims in light of the disclosure (claimed disclosure) and avoid deciding on the 'real invention' beyond the record; (D) choose the OR subclass as the most indented subclass of the first subclass array; (E) location of the U.S. patents constituting the prior art is generally controlling; (F) ordinarily cannot assign to a class that includes one element of a claimed combination only — treat the claim in its entirety; (G) an examiner seeking transfer may perform searches of both classes and include results in the transfer record.
